When success knocks on Fahmida’s door
item.description:
“While returning from school my daughter said, she wanted to take a rickshaw home. I told her we had no money. My son said he wanted a banana. I brought him home, saying I would buy one later. I felt heartbroken. I asked, Allah, why are you making us suffer so much?”

On 25 June 2014, Fahmida Jannat (Happy) of Sylhet recorded this bitter experience from her life in her diary. Twelve years later, on 26 June 2026, Fahmida wrote on her Facebook status, “Every hardship, every busy moment and every small success teaches me to become stronger. Love your work. In Shaa Allah, success will knock on your door one day.”

Success has also knocked on Fahmida’s door. She is now financially independent. She says, “I managed to survive because I was patient, honest and hardworking. Otherwise, I would have been swept away like a piece of straw long ago!”

Lubana Yesmin, president of the Sylhet Women Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said Fahmida’s life story “surpasses even a movie”. She told Prothom Alo that Fahmida’s husband suddenly left her, leaving her with their two children.

After years of relentless hard work and dedication, she eventually succeeded in life. The eventful tale of this successful woman entrepreneur now inspires others.

The life she left behind

Fahmida rents the second floor of a house in Mirabazar in Sylhet city. She spoke to this reporter at the house on the evening of 9 June. During the conversation, Fahmida brought out several diaries and showed them to the correspondent. Page after page of these diaries contains her account of the life she left behind.

According to Fahmida, her family home is in Beanibazar, Sylhet. In 2007, her family arranged her marriage to a bank official from Dargah Gate in Sylhet city. She had only recently completed her Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) examination at the time. She spent the first two and a half years of her marriage relatively happily. Suddenly, her in-laws began treating her badly. At one point, her husband also began behaving badly towards her.

How happiness came into her life

Fahmida says, “I knew how to sew and do block printing and batik work. I put those skills to use in 2017. I would take my daughter to school and bring various sewing orders from other parents home, completing the work there. That is how I started earning. Later, with financial support from my siblings, I started a clothing business, sewing all sorts of garments.”

At the time, her in-laws taunted her with various remarks, including calling her “shelai apa”. Unable to discourage her, her in-laws took other measures. Alongside threats and pressure to leave home, they disconnected her water supply and gas connection and frequently harassed and intimidated her by sending groups of people to her home at night, posing as her husband’s “creditors”.

Police also regularly came to the house after allegations of a “cheque forgery case” were brought against her husband. This frightened the children. Living constantly in fear and anxiety, both her daughter and son began to develop mental health problems. Fahmida herself suffered a stroke in 2019. She later rented a house in Mirabazar in the city in 2021 and began a new life.

After moving into the rented house, Fahmida launched an online page and YouTube channel called “Happy’s Kitchen”. She began supplying a variety of healthy and tasty homemade food. Her reputation grew steadily because of the quality of her food, and she now regularly supplies food to various organisations and events.

For about two years after she began supplying food through her online page, Fahmida prepared and delivered cooked meals every day to a popular online-based food and grocery delivery company for a monthly payment of Tk 10,000. She left the job after her own online page became popular. Her business is now well known.

Prosperity and happiness

In 2024, Fahmida received an award plaque from the Entrepreneur and E-Commerce Platform. Her children are also doing well in their studies. Her daughter passed this year’s secondary examination with an ‘A’ grade, while her son is studying in Class Eight.

Fahmida has hired an assistant for “Happy’s Kitchen” at a monthly salary of Tk 3,000. Five temporary delivery workers also work for the business. Her current income allows her to cover rent, household expenses, her children’s education and other needs, while leaving her with more than Tk 5,000 each month.

Fahmida now fills her diary with accounts of happiness and stories of joy. She has only one thing to say: “I do not want to look back anymore. My only goal now is to keep moving forward.”

item.title: Dhaka health centre demolition: 4 arrested
item.description:
Shah Ali police have arrested four people over the vandalism and looting at the Radda MCH-FP Centre in Mirpur-1 in the capital at midnight after tying up security guards.

Officer-in-Charge (OC) of Shah Ali police station Jahangir Alam confirmed the information on Saturday afternoon. The arrested individuals are Md Sohel, 22, Md Juel, 23, Jihad Hasan, 21, and Md Rabbi, 20.

Health centre demolished at midnight in Dhaka

Jahangir Alam told Prothom Alo that the four were arrested in a raid on Friday night for their involvement in the attack. They confessed to their involvement. They were sent to court. The drive to arrest those involved is still ongoing.

It has been learnt that three of the four arrested people are floating people from Shah Ali Mazar. They took part in the vandalism in exchange for money.

Attack, looting and vandalism

At around midnight last Thursday, the Radda MCH-FP Centre in Mirpur-1 was vandalised and looted. More than 200 masked people allegedly entered the centre with locally made weapons and held two security guards hostage.

They later looted valuable equipment, medicines, vaccines, cash and other goods. The entire facility was then demolished using heavy machinery, including one concrete and three semi-concrete buildings.

The organisation said a case had been filed with Shah Ali police station over the incident. Executive Director of the centre Nasrin Akhter said they had not yet received a copy of the case statement.

The Radda MCH-FP Centre began operations in Mirpur in 1974 to provide maternal and child healthcare to disadvantaged and low-income people in the area. The organisation currently provides various services, including child vaccination, child healthcare, reproductive health and family planning.

item.title: Climbing high and sleeping low: On the Road to Mount Elbrus, Day Two
item.description:
Ikramul Hasan Shakil is Bangladesh's Everest summiteer with the unique distinction of having conquered both the Great Himalaya Trail and the Sea to Summit challenge. He has set off on a new expedition, this time to Mount Elbrus, the highest peak in Europe, located in Russia's Caucasus range. Sidratul Safayat Daniel brings the story of this challenging expedition in a series of dispatches.

On the second day, Shakil and his team remained at Cheget. But today''s target was higher up toward Garabashi. Known as Europe's highest cable car station. Garabashi sits at an altitude of roughly 3,847 metres.

Interestingly, Elbrus actually has two summits, the West Peak (5,642 metres) and the East Peak (5,621 metres). Both are summits of the same dormant volcano. Most mountaineers aim for the higher of the two, the West Peak.

On the Road to Mount Elbrus: Day One

There is a simple rule in mountaineering "climb high, sleep low." The idea is to climb as high as possible during the day, then descend to a comparatively lower altitude to sleep at night. This is how the body gradually adjusts to air. Shakil's acclimatisation process on Day Two followed exactly this principle. The day before, the team had trekked and climbed up to about 4,500 metres.

The weather held up reasonably well at the start of the day's climb, but conditions turned abruptly as they gained altitude. Heavy snowfall, fierce wind and a whiteout. A dangerous mountain condition where cloud, snow and fog merge into a wall of white so thick that the line between sky and ground disappears, making it hard even to hold a direction.

In Shakil's words, the gusts felt strong enough to sweep them off their feet, and the snow stung his face like pinpricks. He said conditions this severe, at such a comparatively low altitude are rare even in the Himalayas. He noted Elbrus has its own temperament.

The Caucasus range is known for its unpredictable weather, where moist air off the Black Sea collides with cold currents from Europe and can change the scene in an instant.

Despite the conditions, Shakil and his teammates pushed on for about two and a half to three hours and reached 4,500 metres before turning back. They were down at the lodge in Cheget by 2 pm. This marked their final acclimatisation day before the summit push. According to the plan, the team will attempt the summit on the night of 24 September.

Shakil and his teammates spent the rest of the afternoon resting, giving their bodies time to recover. This rest period is crucial in avoiding weather sickness.

Many expeditions pay the compensation later for rushing the ascent, which is why experienced mountaineers always advise listening to the body before pushing forward.

item.title: Travel abroad on a low budget: Key tips for smart travelers
item.description:
Sometimes, it is possible to travel abroad at a cost close to what one might spend on a trip to Cox’s Bazar or Sajek. However, doing so requires advance planning. From planning the trip to returning home, being mindful of a few things can significantly reduce the cost of travelling abroad. How much you can save depends on factors such as your travel plan, timing, destination and bookings.

A significant portion of the total budget for an international trip goes towards transportation, particularly airfare. For example, a round-trip ticket from Dhaka to Egypt may cost Tk 90,000. Once there, accommodation, food and sightseeing may cost less than they would in Bangladesh. As a result, airfare can account for a large share of the total travel expenses.

The first way to reduce airfare is to plan ahead. Airlines operating flights from Bangladesh offer special deals from time to time. Subscribing to airlines’ newsletters or promotional messages can help travellers learn about these offers early.

The earlier the travel dates are decided, the more opportunity there is to compare different fares. Buying tickets at the last minute can mean paying higher prices.

Besides travel agencies, travellers can also check offers from online travel agencies, or OTAs, such as GoZayaan. Discounts are sometimes available on these platforms through cards issued by different banks and financial institutions. International booking platforms such as Trip.com also offer ticket deals from time to time. However, before making transactions in foreign currency, it is important to check the relevant bank rules and regulations governing foreign currency use in Bangladesh. At present, bank approval is required to purchase tickets costing more than $300.

Visa processing

A visa is an important consideration when travelling abroad. Visa applications for many countries have to be submitted through designated agencies. For some countries, however, applicants can apply online themselves or submit applications at designated visa centres.

For countries where self-application is allowed, travellers can apply themselves after learning the required documents and procedures. This can help save on agency service charges.

However, visa requirements vary from country to country. There is plenty of related content available on YouTube, and AI tools can also provide a general overview of the process. For the actual application, however, applicants should always follow the latest instructions issued by the relevant embassy, consulate or official government visa website.

From the airport to the hotel

Getting from the airport to the hotel can be one of the first major expenses after arriving in a new country. Airports in most cities are located some distance from the main city. Taking a taxi or private car can increase the cost further. Depending on the country, the expense can range from Tk 3,000 to Tk 15,000.

It is therefore better to plan the route from the airport to the hotel before travelling. Some cities have airport metro services, while others offer buses or shuttle services. These options can get travellers into the city at a much lower cost than taxis.

Some hotels also offer free or paid airport transfer services. Travellers can check whether such a service is available when making a hotel reservation.

Hotel booking

One of the easiest ways to reduce hotel costs is to compare prices across different platforms in advance. Online platforms such as Booking.com, Agoda and Trip.com allow travellers to compare prices, locations, facilities and guest reviews of hotels in the same area.

Booking a hotel about a month before the trip can help travellers find options within their budget. However, a hotel should not be selected solely on the basis of price. Its location should also be considered. Choosing a cheap hotel far outside the city can result in additional daily transportation costs that may outweigh the savings on accommodation.

Therefore, choosing a hotel near public transport and with easy access to tourist attractions can help reduce the overall cost of the trip.

Tickets for tours and attractions

Travellers often need to buy separate tickets for tourist attractions, museums, rides and day tours abroad. In some cases, booking online in advance can offer discounts. Combo packages covering multiple attractions may also be available at lower prices.

Platforms such as Klook offer tour, attraction and ride packages in various destinations. However, before booking, it is advisable to compare the price with that listed on the attraction’s official website. Travellers should also check what is included in the package, the cancellation policy and whether there are any additional charges.

item.title: Old gangs remain active, drawing in youth from affluent families
item.description:
Assistant Revenue Officer Bullet Bairagi was returning to Cumilla on the night of 24 April after completing training in Chattogram. On the way, he boarded a CNG-run auto-rickshaw.

According to the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), robbers had disguised themselves as the driver and a passenger. After assaulting him and taking his mobile phone, money and bag, they threw him from the moving auto-rickshaw.

The following morning, authorities recovered his body beside the highway near the Irish Hill Hotel in Kotbari.

Police had arrested one of the accused in the murder from the railway line area nearly two months earlier. He was later released on bail.

A source at the Special Response Battalion (SRB), which replaced RAB, said the person belonged to a robbery gang known locally as a teenage gang.

Cumilla has seen several other cases in which people were arrested earlier, released on bail and later accused of committing new crimes.

Prothom Alo reviewed information on 32 incidents and operations involving teen gang activities and related organised crimes. The names of old gangs repeatedly appeared in clashes, displays of weapons and attacks.

A recently released video showed the leader of the Ratan Group staging a show of force in front of the police superintendent’s office. Meanwhile, some families are struggling after their children became involved with teenage gangs.

From 7 March 2023 to 23 September this year, the published figures for those detained and arrested in these incidents and operations total 881. We also reviewed earlier information to understand the previous activities of several individuals.

The review found that the same areas and gang names repeatedly appeared, while old accused individuals faced allegations of involvement in new crimes.

Arrested before, accused again

Nilima Bairagi, the mother of Assistant Revenue Officer Bullet Bairagi, filed a case with Sadar South model police station over his murder. RAB arrested five people.

According to the SRB source, one of them had been arrested in an earlier case, released and later became involved in crime again.

On 3 June 2025, police arrested Rakibul Hasan Riad, Sohag Molla and Khairul Hasan on allegations of preparing to commit robbery in the Tomsom Bridge area.

According to police, Riad and Sohag had been released on bail that evening, while Khairul had secured bail about a month earlier.

Nayan Hossain, also known as Nayan Bond, was a prominent figure in teenage gang activities in Cumilla city.

In December 2022, he faced seven cases at Kotwali and Sadar South model police stations. He was in prison at the time. Four people arrested from the BSCIC industrial area with weapons, crude bombs and drugs were his associates, according to the information available then.

On the night of 3 December 2024, a group called Sajib Hossain, also known as Babu, out of his home in the Ashoktala railway crossing area, assaulted and stabbed him. He died in hospital the following day.

Nayan, Chayan and their associates were named in the case. Police said a dispute linked to teenage gangs and drug trafficking lay behind the incident.

Local residents said Nayan is now in the area. A local source claimed that he still leads the gang. An inquiry also found that Point Rabbi, who was arrested in 2023, is currently in the area.

Ratan seen in rally led by Chhatra Dal leader

Police sources said Imran Hossain, also known as Ratan, the leader of the Ratan Group who was arrested in April 2025, is currently out on bail. Several videos of him were posted on social media on Wednesday.

The videos showed a group including Ratan staging a show of force in front of the district police superintendent’s office. Md Mohsin, vice-president of Cumilla Metropolitan Chhatra Dal, was leading the group.

Mohsin told Prothom Alo that Chhatra Dal was responsible for maintaining discipline at an event organised by the Jubo Dal. He said he was going there with his followers and that many people were part of the procession.

He said he did not know how members of teen gangs had joined them. He said, “We have no involvement with teen gangs.”

Md Nahiduzzaman Rana, president of Cumilla City Chhatra Dal, told Prothom Alo that they had always been campaigning against teenage gangs and drugs. He said he contacted the vice-president after watching the video.

According to Rana, the vice-president said he had not known about the involvement of teenage gang members. He added that they were still investigating the matter and would take organisational action if they found any involvement.

Old gang member, attempt to form a new gang

On the afternoon of 18 September, 13-year-old schoolboy Ishayat Shahriar Apratim was taken to a secluded forest in the Sananda area of Lalmai Hills and killed.

Local residents said the two teenagers, including arrested suspect Saiful Islam Tuhin, were members of a gang called RZ-36. Local sources also said Tuhin had recently been trying to form his own gang in the Kotbari and university areas.

Several sources involved in the investigation said the two teenagers had been involved in various incidents, including staging motorcycle rallies to create fear.

Police said the suspects took Apratim to the secluded area to snatch his iPhone. They also allegedly lured him with the promise of making a TikTok video.

Same gangs, repeated violence

A review of 32 incidents identified 12 teenage gangs and sub-groups: Ratan or R Squad, Eagle, CBK, CBK Danger Zone, CBK Junior, CBK Special, RDX, RZ-36, CDX, King Squad, Red 999 and BGM. If CBK and its three aforementioned sub-groups are treated as one network, the number of gangs comes to nine. Information from various incidents also linked gangs led by Point Rabbi, Tajul Islam Suman and Nayan Bond.

The names Ratan and Eagle emerged in connection with a clash in February 2024 and a rally in January 2025. In April that year, various groups also staged shows of strength while carrying weapons.

Following rallies on 25 April at the banks of Rani’s Dighi, Talpukurpaar and Adalatpara, police initially arrested five people and later arrested nine more. A further nine people were arrested in a joint operation by the army and RAB. The total number of arrests was 23.

In October of the same year, following a clash at Victoria College, police arrested 16 people while the then-RAB arrested eight.

The two incidents resulted in 47 arrests. In both cases, public violence or weapons displays preceded the major operations.

In August 2025, when police detained 21 members of King Squad from the KTC field in the Housing area, they said the group had announced the rally on social media and was preparing to stage it.

In the same month, police detained 27 members of RDX and CDX for allegedly preparing to stage a rally.

Despite the word “teenage” in their names, not all members of the groups are minors. The published ages of the nine people detained during a joint operation in April 2025 ranged from 19 to 47. RAB had identified one of them as a weapons supplier.

Five murders, others also targeted in attacks

The review covered five murder cases: Apritim, Bullet, Hridoy, Badhan and Sajib, also known as Babu. In the Hridoy murder in Chauddagram, local residents gave a different account of the motive for the dispute from the findings of the police’s preliminary investigation.

Local residents described Badhan, a dismissed police constable who was killed in Daudkandi on 23 April 2023, as a gang leader. Information later showed that police arrested three people in the case.

People have also fallen victim to attacks despite having no involvement in the disputes. Members of a teenage gang attacked police officer Kazi Abdullah Md Zubayer at the banks of Dharmasagar after he protested against indecent remarks about his wife.

Schoolboy Ethan Ahmed was shot amid a dispute between two drug-related groups in Katabil. Police said they arrested four people and recovered a pistol and ammunition.

Families helpless over their children

A common perception is that teenage gangs generally involve children from poor families and those living in slums. Although Cumilla has seen cases involving children from such families, gang activities are not confined to them.

Information shows that children from socially established families, including those of government employees, have also come into contact with and become involved in such groups.

A government official working in land administration in Debidwar had to send his child to a rehabilitation centre after the child became involved with a gang and developed a drug addiction.

The official said the child’s behaviour had caused the family to face social humiliation. Speaking on condition of anonymity, he said, “My child has become involved with these teenage gang groups, become addicted to drugs and is heading towards destruction. I feel completely helpless.”

In his view, criminal activities similar to those of teenage gangs have now spread to rural areas as well.

On 20 May in Debidwar, the two gangs known as “Red 999” and “BGM” allegedly engaged in a public display of weapons and attacks amid a dispute between them.

Police detained 20 people and released 12 after verification and questioning. They showed eight as arrested in the case and produced them before a court the following day. The investigation found information linking the official’s child to these groups.

A law enforcement source said officers recently contacted the parents of several people they detained after finding them travelling together on motorcycles.

The parents included people from locally known families, including one lawyer. Most of them could not say where their children were. One father said, “I do not know where my son is; his mother may know.”

Major Sadman Ibne Alam, deputy director and company commander of SRB-11 CPC-2, Cumilla, told Prothom Alo that law enforcement agencies had arrested many gang members through a series of operations.

However, he said families have the most important role in preventing juvenile crime. If parents remain attentive and keep track of where their children are and whom they associate with, he said, resolving the problem becomes easier.

On 23 September, police conducted simultaneous operations across the district’s 18 police stations and detained 624 people.

item.title: Four arrested over attack on Radda healthcare center
item.description:
Police arrested four people on Saturday in connection with an attack, looting and vandalism at the Radda MCH-FP Centre, a low-cost healthcare facility in Mirpur, Dhaka.
Shah Ali Police Station Officer-in-Charge Jahangir Alam confirmed the arrests on Saturday, saying the suspects were detained from different parts of the capital.
The incident took place around midnight on Thursday at the Radda MCH-FP Centre in Mirpur Section-1. The following day, the clinic’s Executive Director Nasrin Akhtar filed a case with Shah Ali Police Station.
The case names Hanif Mia as an accused and includes around 250 unidentified individuals.
According to clinic authorities, more than 200 masked individuals entered the facility after holding security guards hostage. They allegedly looted medical equipment, medicines, government vaccines, cash and other valuables.
The authorities also claimed that the attackers used heavy machinery to demolish one concrete building and three semi-permanent structures on the premises after the looting.
They estimated the total damage caused by the attack, looting and vandalism at around Tk 15 million.
The clinic further alleged that a signboard bearing the name “Somomona Dokandar Samity Ltd” was installed at the site after the attack.
It also claimed that police were present at the scene during the incident but did not take immediate action.
Following the incident, law enforcement agencies increased their security presence around the Radda MCH-FP Centre.

item.title: Health minister: Measles vaccination delay behind child deaths
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain blamed a four-year delay and negligence in the measles vaccination program during the tenure of the ousted Awami League government and the interim government for the recent deaths of children.
“The death of every child is deeply painful and a matter of shame for the government,” he said after inaugurating the second phase of the measles vaccination campaign at Korail TNT playground in Banani on Saturday.
The health minister said the nation had to pay the price for the previous government’s prolonged delay and negligence in importing vaccines from abroad, citing the suspension of the vaccination program and excuses over the open tender system.
Expressing deep sympathy, he said around 1,000 children died of measles out of nearly 18.5 million children.
“The nation has had to pay the price for the prolonged delay and negligence. Many mothers have lost their children,”he added.
The current government, after taking charge, took swift measures and successfully implemented a large-scale nationwide vaccination campaign, said the minister.
The nationwide measles vaccination campaign targeting 34 lakh children aged six months to 59 months began on Saturday and will continue until October 31.
The government launched the vaccination campaign in three phases from April 5 after assuming responsibility, and since April 20, the nationwide campaign has vaccinated around 1.85 crore children, he said.
The government has also set a target to vaccinate an additional 3.4 million children who were missed during the campaign.
Some ten lakh vaccine doses have also been kept in reserve for emergency needs, and vaccination with these doses will continue alongside the routine immunisation program, he said.

item.title: Bangladesh, US sign strategic civil nuclear cooperation agreement
item.description:
Bangladesh and the United States have signed a strategic agreement on civil nuclear cooperation, marking a new step in bilateral cooperation in the peaceful use of nuclear technology.
Prime Minister’s Adviser for Science and Technology Rehan Asad signed the agreement on behalf of Bangladesh, while US Secretary Jacob Helberg signed it on behalf of the US on September 25, the BNP media cell said in a post on its verified Facebook page.
During US Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor's recent visit, Washington proposed a memorandum of understanding on civil nuclear cooperation with Bangladesh.
On August 3, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said Bangladesh views the US proposal on civil nuclear cooperation positively, stressing that any engagement with Washington will be considered if it serves the interests of the people of Bangladesh.
She said the government's approach remains “positive”, and any bilateral agreement with the United States will be considered based on Bangladesh's national interest.

item.title: Nationwide measles-rubella catch-up vaccination drive launched
item.description:
The government has launched an intensified nationwide measles-rubella catch-up vaccination campaign targeting 3.4 million children aged 6-59 months who missed previous doses.
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Hossain inaugurated the campaign at the TNT ground in Mohakhali on Saturday.
Speaking at the inauguration, the minister said 18,500,833 children had so far been vaccinated under the nationwide measles-rubella program.
He said the country’s measles situation had become critical following a prolonged gap in vaccination.
“Malnutrition rates are high among children infected with measles. Malnourished children who contract measles quickly develop pneumonia and fall into critical condition,” he said.
Medical experts identify pneumonia and malnutrition as among the leading causes of death among children infected with measles, he added.
The minister said the vaccination program began on April 5 after he assumed office. In the first phase, activities were conducted in 18 districts in three stages, as designated by Unicef.
Dhaka and two other major city corporations were later brought under the program, while the nationwide campaign was expanded ahead of schedule from April 20.
He said the number of measles infections had increased because of the vaccination gap, with around 1,000 children dying during the period.
“The death of even a single child is deeply tragic. It inflicts irreparable loss upon a family,” he said.
The minister said 22.5 million children were covered under the Vitamin A capsule programme, compared with around 18.5 million who received measles-rubella vaccines.
To address the gap of around 4 million children, an initiative was launched to identify those who had missed vaccination. Around 1.4 million children were subsequently identified and vaccinated.
However, as measles has not yet been brought fully under control, the government has launched the latest catch-up campaign, he said.
Unicef supplied an additional 4 million vaccine doses within 10 days, the minister said.
Combining the new supply with existing stocks, the current campaign targets 3.4 million children, including 1 million infants and 2.4 million children who previously missed vaccination.
Vaccination activities have been intensified from Saturday through camps in every union across the country.
Activities at the upazila level will be coordinated by the local administration, civil surgeons, upazila nirbahi officers (UNOs) and health workers.
Vaccines will also be administered on holidays to accommodate working mothers, while vaccination activities will continue after sunset, the minister said.
The campaign aims to cover all children aged 6-59 months.
Around 1 million vaccine doses are expected to remain in stock after the current campaign, he said.
So far, 4.3 million doses have been distributed among various upazilas, and the remaining supplies will be preserved for future programmes.
The minister said Bangladeshi medical professionals had consistently demonstrated dedication during epidemics and other emergencies.
Given Bangladesh’s high population density, measles can spread rapidly, with children easily becoming infected through contact with an infected child, he said.
He urged all stakeholders, including the media, to cooperate in ensuring the success of the vaccination campaign.

item.title: When will Bangla take its place at the UN?
item.description:
There are moments in a nation's history when a language becomes much more than a means of communication. It becomes a symbol of identity, dignity, and collective struggle. For Bangladesh, Bangla is precisely such a language.
The blood shed during the Language Movement of 1952 transformed the demand for linguistic rights into one of the defining chapters of the nation's history. More than seven decades later, the question is no longer whether Bangla has a place in the global linguistic landscape. It is whether that place can now be reflected in the world's foremost multilateral institution -- the United Nations.
The United Nations began its journey in 1945 with five official languages: English, French, Russian, Spanish, and Mandarin (Chinese). Arabic was added in 1973, bringing the total number of official UN languages to six. Initially, only English and French were used as the working languages of the Security Council from 1946. Russian and Spanish were added in 1969, while Mandarin was adopted for that purpose in 1974. Although Arabic became an official UN language in 1973, its use in the Security Council began only in 1982.
Spanish is the official language of 20 countries worldwide, most of which are located in Latin America -- specifically Central America, the Caribbean, and South America. However, although Spanish is widely spoken in the United States, it is not the country's federal official language.
The history of these languages offers an important perspective on the question of Bangla. Russian and Spanish waited 23 years after the establishment of the United Nations before becoming Security Council languages, while Mandarin waited 29 years. Arabic, by contrast, was adopted as a Security Council language nine years after becoming an official UN language.
The official languages of all five permanent members of the Security Council (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) are also UN languages. At the same time, no Arab country or Muslim-majority member of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) has yet secured a permanent seat on the Security Council.
Although Bangla ranks sixth worldwide in terms of the number of speakers, it enjoys official-language status in only a limited number of jurisdictions. Russian, ranking eighth, has attained official UN language status, bypassing Bangla (ranked sixth) and Portuguese (ranked seventh).
Historically, imperial powers extended the influence of their languages in tandem with the expansion of their empires. Today, four European languages are among the official languages of the United Nations, while English serves as the official language of both the United Kingdom and the United States. Arabic, meanwhile, holds official status in numerous countries across Africa and the Middle East. Against this historical and geopolitical backdrop, the inclusion of another major Asian language remains an unresolved issue.
Bangladesh's heads of state or heads of government deliver speeches in Bangla at the United Nations General Assembly every year. Bangla's international profile received a major boost in 1999, when UNESCO proclaimed February 21 International Mother Language Day. What began as a commemoration of the language martyrs of Bangladesh has since become a global observance of linguistic diversity and the right to speak one's mother tongue.
The recognition gave Bangladesh a unique opportunity to place Bangla within a broader international discourse on language, culture, and identity. Yet international recognition and institutional recognition are not the same thing.
The price of recognition
One of the most frequently cited obstacles to making Bangla an official UN language is cost. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has previously indicated that Bangladesh would need to commit at least $60 million annually to meet the additional expenses, particularly for translation and interpretation within the UN system.
By comparison, Bangladesh currently contributes approximately $300,000 a year to the UN budget, or around 0.1% of the total.
The financial challenge is therefore substantial. But technology may have changed the nature of that challenge. Artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed machine translation at a speed that would have been difficult to imagine even a decade ago.
The UN's enormous volume of documents, reports, statements, and communications requires translation between its six official languages. Extending such services to Bangla would undoubtedly require considerable investment, technical safeguards, and human oversight.
But the development of AI-assisted translation systems could potentially reduce the recurring cost substantially. Instead of viewing the $60 million figure as an unavoidable permanent expenditure, Bangladesh could explore whether an initial investment in research, development, language datasets, and AI-powered translation infrastructure could create a more sustainable model.
Such a system would still require professional translators and institutional quality control, particularly for diplomatic, legal, and technical documents. But technology could make the financial equation considerably more manageable.
This is where Bangladesh's growing information technology sector could become strategically important. The issue, therefore, should not be framed solely as a question of how much Bangladesh would have to pay. It should also be framed as a question of how Bangladesh can use its technological capabilities to reduce the cost of linguistic inclusion.
A language of more than 350 million people
The demographic case for Bangla is substantial. More than 350 million people around the world speak Bangla, placing it among the world's major languages. Yet the number of speakers alone does not determine whether a language becomes an official UN language.
Hindi, for example, has hundreds of millions of speakers but is not an official UN language. Russian, despite having considerably fewer speakers, already enjoys official status.
India's linguistic structure also makes a direct comparison between Hindi and Bangla more complicated. India has no single national language. The Constitution recognizes 22 languages, while individual states have their own official languages and English continues to play a major role in administration, higher education, and interstate communication.
Of course, international linguistic influence depends on much more than population. Political reach, economic relevance, geographic distribution, cultural influence, diplomatic utility, and institutional capacity all matter. That is why the question of Bangla's future at the UN cannot be reduced to a simple calculation of how many people speak it.
Bangla beyond Bangladesh
Bangla's geographical reach is far greater than Bangladesh alone. In addition to being the principal language of Bangladesh, Bangla is widely spoken in India, particularly in West Bengal, Tripura and Assam, as well as in other parts of eastern India.
Bangla-speaking communities also exist in Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Myanmar. Large Bangladeshi and Bangla-speaking communities have emerged across the Middle East, particularly in the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Qatar.
Beyond Asia and the Middle East, Bangla is spoken by substantial communities in the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Germany, Australia, and Japan. This global diaspora represents an important but underutilized resource for the internationalisation of Bangla.
For millions of expatriate Bengalis, Bangla remains the language of family, culture, and community. Over the past 25 years, Bangladeshi expatriate organizations in different cities around the world have submitted memoranda to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Cultural Affairs, Bangladesh's diplomatic missions, and the United Nations, calling for Bangla to be recognized as an official UN language.
What appears to be missing is a sustained, coordinated international campaign bringing these individual efforts together under a clearly defined national strategy.
Portuguese presents another useful comparison. With a global population of speakers broadly comparable to Bengali, Portuguese is used across at least 12 countries, including Portugal and Brazil, and has an established presence alongside Spanish across Europe, Latin America, and other parts of the world.
Malay is another language with a substantial regional footprint. It is spoken in Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Brunei, Timor-Leste, and parts of Thailand.
Arabic offers perhaps the most relevant precedent. It became an official UN language after the Arab states concerned agreed to shoulder the full cost of translating UN documents into Arabic.
Its recognition was therefore supported not simply by the number of speakers but by a coordinated political commitment among a group of states.
That precedent carries a clear lesson for Bangladesh: International linguistic recognition requires diplomacy, institutional preparedness, and financial commitment in addition to a large speaker population.
The global importance of a language can also be measured through economic and geopolitical influence. Approximately 1.5 billion people worldwide speak English, followed by Mandarin with around 1.1 billion, Hindi with approximately 600 million, Spanish with about 550 million, Arabic with around 370 million, Bengali with approximately 350 million, French with around 270 million, and Russian around 250 million.
But when language is assessed through economic and geopolitical power, the ranking changes. The World Economic Forum's "Power Language Index" places English, Mandarin, French, Spanish, Arabic, Russian, German, Japanese, Portuguese, and Hindi among the world's most influential languages.
The index considers factors such as economic opportunity, access to knowledge and media, geographic diplomacy, travel, and the ability to facilitate dialogue. Bangla's challenge, therefore, is not a lack of speakers. It is the comparatively limited economic and institutional power associated with the language outside its traditional geographic base. That is something Bangladesh can change.
Bangla has already acquired an extraordinary cultural legacy. Rabindranath Tagore became the first Asian Nobel laureate, receiving the Nobel Prize in Literature. Amartya Sen received the Nobel Prize in Economics, while Dr Muhammad Yunus received the Nobel Peace Prize. Bengali literature, music, cinema, and scholarship have continued to attract international audiences.
Bangla-language media have also expanded beyond Bangladesh and India. Bangla programs have been broadcast through radio and television in countries including the United States, the United Kingdom, Russia, Germany, China, Japan, the Philippines, Iran, and Pakistan. Bengali newspapers and online media platforms are published across the world, while the use of Bangla on the internet has grown significantly.
UN Radio launched Bangla-language programming in 2012, although the service was suspended in 2021 amid budget constraints during the Covid-19 pandemic. The UNDP has also published its annual report on Asia in Bangla alongside the English edition.
Meanwhile, Bangladesh's diplomatic community has been using language as a form of cultural diplomacy. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs organizes events in Dhaka to mark International Mother Language Day, with representatives of foreign missions participating. Diplomats posted in Bangladesh pay tribute to the language martyrs by laying flowers at a temporary Shaheed Minar at the Foreign Service Academy.
Some foreign diplomats posted in Dhaka have also taken up learning Bangla. These developments demonstrate that the internationalization of Bangla is already taking place, albeit incrementally and without a sufficiently coordinated strategy.
For Bangla to become an official language of the United Nations, Bangladesh would need to formally place the issue before the General Assembly and seek support for a resolution.
Such an initiative would require extensive diplomatic engagement with other member states. But diplomacy should not begin with the resolution. It should begin much earlier. It is worth noting that Bangladesh is presiding over the current session of the United Nations General Assembly.
Bangladesh would first need to build a broad coalition of countries and international organizations willing to support the initiative. It would need to demonstrate that the financial and technological requirements of incorporating Bangla into the UN system can be met.
It would also need to establish a credible institutional mechanism for translation, interpretation, terminology development, and quality control. Most importantly, the government would need to treat the issue as a long-term state policy rather than an occasional diplomatic initiative.
There is no simple population-based formula for determining which languages become official UN languages. The existing six official languages themselves demonstrate that geopolitical history, diplomatic influence, and international utility have played a major role.
Bangla is one of South Asia's major languages. Its history is inseparable from one of the world's most significant struggles for linguistic rights. Its literature has produced globally recognized figures. Its speakers span continents. Its digital presence is expanding. And its symbolic importance has already been acknowledged by the international community through International Mother Language Day.
Bangla has a history worthy of international recognition. But the question is whether Bangladesh can convert that historical and cultural capital into sustained diplomatic, technological, and economic influence.
Recognition at the United Nations would undoubtedly carry symbolic importance. It could enhance the international visibility of Bangla, strengthen Bangladesh's cultural identity, and make communication between Bengali speakers and international institutions easier.
But official recognition alone would not guarantee the global expansion of a language. Languages thrive when people have reasons to learn and use them.
That means Bangladesh must simultaneously increase the economic, technological, and cultural value of Bangla. Electronic and digital media can play a major role. Bengali cinema, drama, music, literature, publishing, educational content, software, and AI applications can all contribute to expanding the language's global reach.
The commercialization of Bangla should not be seen as a threat to its cultural identity. Rather, economic utility can reinforce cultural influence. A language that becomes useful in education, technology, entertainment, business, and international communication is more likely to cross borders and attract new learners. This is perhaps the most important lesson for Bangladesh.
The struggle for Bangla began with a demand for linguistic dignity. It evolved into a defining element of national identity.
The next stage requires a different kind of movement -- one built not only on emotion and historical memory, but also on diplomacy, technology, investment, cultural production, and economic opportunity.
Seventy years after Bangla became the state language of Pakistan's eastern wing and more than seven decades after the Language Movement, Bangladesh has an opportunity to take the language's global journey to another level.
Making Bangla an official language of the United Nations may be a long and difficult process. It may require years of diplomacy, substantial investment, and considerable institutional preparation. But the ambition itself is neither unrealistic nor misplaced.
If Bangladesh wants Bangla to speak more prominently on the world stage, it must first give the language the economic, technological, and diplomatic strength to be heard. The time has come to move from commemorating the language to strategically investing in its future.
Salahuddin Ahmaad Bablu is a senior journalist.

item.title: AI didn't give me sight. It gave me independence
item.description:
A few months ago, I received a phone call from a mother who is blind. She was not calling to discuss technology. She was calling because she was worried about her two-year-old son.
"My son has learned that I cannot see," she told me. "He has also learned that if he stays completely quiet, I cannot find him. Sometimes he hides in a corner of the room without making a sound. Those are the moments that frighten me the most."
As she spoke, I could hear something that every parent understands: Fear for a child's safety. But for her, that fear was magnified by the simple reality that she could not rely on vision.
I suggested she try an AI-powered visual assistance app. Using the smartphone's camera, the app analyzes the surroundings and describes them aloud in real time.
A few weeks later, she called me again.
This time, her voice sounded different.
"My phone tells me, 'Your child is standing near the door.' It says, 'Your child is playing with a toy.' Sometimes it even tells me what he is holding. I can find him almost immediately."
The technology had not restored her eyesight.
But it had restored something equally important: Confidence.
That conversation stayed with me because it perfectly captured what artificial intelligence really means for many persons with disabilities.
Public discussions about AI usually focus on automation, productivity, investment, or whether machines will replace human jobs. Those conversations are important. Yet they often overlook another reality.
For millions of people with disabilities, AI is not about replacing people. It is about reducing dependence.
I know this because I live it every day.
I am a person with a visual disability, and for much of my life, ordinary tasks depended on someone else's availability.
If someone handed me a printed document, I had to ask them to read it.
If I received a business card, I had to ask whose name was written on it.
If I wanted to identify the label on a medicine bottle or read information on product packaging, I often needed another person's help.
There is nothing wrong with asking for support. We all depend on one another in different ways.
But when every simple task requires assistance, independence slowly slips away.
Artificial intelligence is changing that.
Today, I begin my mornings by reading the news independently. AI reads newspapers and online articles aloud, allowing me to follow national affairs, global events, and public debates without waiting for someone else to read them to me.
When I prepare for work, AI helps identify the colour of my clothes and suggests matching combinations.
To many people, choosing a shirt may seem insignificant.
To me, choosing my own clothes without asking another person is dignity in action.
Even this article has been shaped with the help of AI.
I speak, AI converts my words into text, and I refine the ideas. What once took hours can now be accomplished far more efficiently, allowing me to spend less time overcoming barriers and more time contributing my expertise.
Across the world, similar stories are unfolding every day.
Students are accessing textbooks more independently.
Professionals are reviewing documents and writing reports.
Entrepreneurs are managing businesses.
People are navigating unfamiliar places with greater confidence.
Families are communicating more effectively.
AI is quietly removing barriers that many people never realized existed.
However, technology alone is not enough. AI can only be transformative when the digital world itself is accessible.
An intelligent assistant cannot fully compensate for a website that cannot be navigated with a screen reader, an online form that is inaccessible from the keyboard, or a mobile application that ignores basic accessibility standards.
Accessibility remains the foundation. AI is an accelerator -- not a substitute -- for inclusive design.
As someone who has spent more than two decades working on digital accessibility, I see AI as one of the greatest opportunities to build a more inclusive society. But that opportunity will only be realized if governments, businesses, educators, developers, and technology companies intentionally include persons with disabilities in designing and testing digital products.
The disability community has long embraced the principle: "Nothing about us without us."
The same principle must guide the future of AI.
When people with disabilities participate in designing technology, AI becomes more accurate, more useful, and ultimately more human.
People sometimes ask me whether AI has changed my life.
My answer is simple.
AI did not give me sight. It gave me something I value just as much.
The freedom to read independently.
The confidence to make my own choices.
The dignity to participate more equally in society.
And for millions of people with disabilities around the world, that may be AI's most remarkable achievement.
Vashkar Bhattacharjee is a digital accessibility expert and disability rights advocate with a visual disability and over 20 years of experience. Email: vashkarbd@gmail.com .

item.title: Putting Bangladesh first
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s address to the 81st United Nations General Assembly was a historic moment for the nation, and we commend how he presented a broad vision for our future.
The speech outlined the values the government says should guide the country’s next chapter: Democracy, equality, accountability, dignity, opportunity, peace, and inclusive development.
The emphasis on rebuilding democratic institutions and ensuring equal rights is particularly significant -- aspiring for a nation where people, regardless of political affiliation, religion, or race, can live safely and with dignity, and where democracy extends across the country.
The focus on young people, women, and children reflects another important part of this vision.
Developing skills, creating employment, encouraging entrepreneurship, expanding women’s education and economic participation, and strengthening education, health and sports could help Bangladesh make better use of its demographic dividend.
If pursued effectively, such priorities could create a society where citizens have greater opportunities to build secure and productive lives.
The speech also placed Bangladesh within a wider global framework: Its calls for peaceful conflict resolution, multilateral cooperation, climate justice, technology transfer, and fair access to artificial intelligence demonstrate an emphasis on cooperation and shared responsibility.
Ultimately, however, the significance of this vision will depend on how firmly these principles take root at home.
Economic inclusion must reach those who have traditionally been left behind. Education and employment opportunities must translate into better prospects for young people, while women and children must be able to benefit from the country’s progress.
The speech has therefore set out an expansive vision of a safer, more democratic, inclusive and self-reliant Bangladesh.
The opportunity now lies in turning that vision into sustained action. If the values outlined at the UN become the foundation of governance and development, they could help shape a future in which progress is measured not only by economic growth, but by how widely security, dignity, and opportunity are shared.

item.title: The case for digital banks
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank’s initial approval for five digital banks is an encouraging development for the country’s financial sector -- a move that can help accelerate the transition towards a more accessible, technology-driven banking system while creating new opportunities for people who remain underserved by conventional banking channels.
The proposed institutions, backed by businesses including bKash, Robi, Banglalink, and Square Group, will operate without conventional branches, providing banking services primarily through digital platforms.
This model could make financial services more convenient, particularly for people and small businesses that face difficulties accessing traditional banking facilities.
Bangladesh has already experienced rapid growth in mobile financial services, making the expansion of digital banking a natural next step.
There is also considerable potential for digital banks to support smaller borrowers and entrepreneurs: According to Bangladesh Bank, the new institutions are expected to focus on underserved customers and smaller loans rather than large-scale lending.
If managed responsibly, this could help broaden access to formal finance and support economic participation among people who have traditionally remained outside the banking system.
At the same time, innovation must be accompanied by strong safeguards. Digital banking will involve the collection and management of significant amounts of financial and personal data, making cybersecurity, consumer protection, and reliable digital infrastructure essential.
Bangladesh Bank must maintain rigorous oversight to ensure that technological convenience does not come at the expense of financial security or public confidence.
It is also important to remember that an initial approval is not a final license. The proposed banks must establish the necessary infrastructure and fulfil regulatory requirements before they can begin operations. This measured approach is welcome.
If the new banks combine innovation with accountability, security, and responsible lending, they could help make Bangladesh’s financial system more inclusive and efficient.
The move, therefore, represents a potentially important step towards a banking sector that better reflects the country’s increasingly digital economy.

item.title: Sheltech Ceramics opens new Experience Center at Sheltech Legacy Plaza
item.description:
Sheltech Ceramics Limited (SCL) opened its newest Experience Center on September 24 at Sheltech Legacy Plaza in Banasree, marking the brand’s third Experience Center in Dhaka.
Located on Banasree’s main road, the new space brings Sheltech Ceramics’ collection of tile products to one of the capital’s rapidly developing residential and commercial areas.
The center is designed as a place where customers can see and experience products in person, from textures and finishes to different combinations and applications.
Speaking about the inauguration, Tanvir Ahmed, managing director, Sheltech Group, said: “Every new Experience Center gives us an opportunity to be closer to our customers and to understand their changing needs. Banasree has developed into an important part of Dhaka, and we see strong potential in this area. With this center, we want to make the Sheltech Ceramics experience more accessible to customers here.”
The new Experience Center is part of Sheltech Legacy Plaza, a newly launched 17-story commercial development on Banasree’s main road.
Its location offers convenient access to Gulshan, Rampura, and Hatirjheel, while planned MRT connectivity is expected to further improve accessibility to the area.
For Sheltech Ceramics, the Banasree opening builds on an expanding network of customer-facing spaces across Dhaka.
SCL already operates Experience Centers in Tejgaon and Hatirpool, each offering customers an opportunity to explore their collections beyond the traditional showroom experience.
Rather than simply displaying products, the new Banasree center has been designed to help customers experience how different tiles and surfaces work together.
This gives homeowners, architects, designers, and project professionals a more direct way to explore options and make decisions based on the actual look and feel of the products.
With its third Dhaka Experience Center now open, Sheltech Ceramics is continuing to expand its physical presence in areas where the city’s residential and commercial landscape is evolving rapidly.

item.title: One killed, 10 injured in Kushtia clash
item.description:
A man was killed and at least 10 others injured in a clash between two groups in Rajapur-Khayerpur area of Kushtia Sadar upazila over establishing dominance in the area on Saturday.
The deceased was identified as Halim Sardar, 60.
According to locals, there was a longstanding dispute between Mannan Member-Bakul group and Yusuf Member-Mehedi group over establishing dominance in the area.
The two groups locked into a series of clashes over the theft of a battery from a local mosque recently.
Against this backdrop, members of the two groups gathered near Chapaigachhi Beel early Saturday and attacked each other, leaving at least 10 people injured.
According to the deceased's family, Halim left his house in the morning and was heading towards Chapaigachhi Beel when a spear-like locally-made weapon was thrown at him from the rooftop of a house belonging to Nazrul, a supporter of Mannan Member.
The weapon struck Halim in the neck, killing him on the spot, they said.
Later, family members rescued him and took him to Kushtia 250-bed General Hospital where doctors declared him dead..
Kushtia Model Police Station Officer-in-Charge Md Zakir Hossain said a suspected has been arrested and police drives are underway to arrest others involved.

item.title: East West University marks 30th founding anniversary
item.description:
East West University (EWU) celebrated its 30th founding anniversary at its campus in Aftabnagar, Dhaka, on September 26, 2026.
The celebration began in the morning with a balloon release attended by members of the Board of Trustees, university administrators, faculty members, students and alumni. A rally followed, circling the campus and surrounding areas.
A reflection session and cultural program were held on the university premises. Professor Dr Shams Rahman, vice-chancellor of EWU, delivered the welcome address.
Professor Dr Anindita Paul spoke on behalf of the faculty members, while Rozina Parvin spoke on behalf of the administrative officers.
The chief guest, Professor Dr Mohammed Farashuddin, founder vice-chancellor and chairperson of the Board of Trustees of EWU, delivered an address highlighting the university’s 30-year journey.
During the reflection session, speakers recounted the history of EWU, which began in September 1996 with 20 students. They highlighted its achievements in education and research over the past three decades and outlined a strategic vision for strengthening the university’s global standing.
Students, alumni and faculty members also performed in a cultural program held during and at the conclusion of the event.
The celebration was attended by members of the Board of Trustees, the pro-vice-chancellor, treasurer, deans of various faculties, department chairs, faculty members, current students and alumni.

item.title: Prof Nurul Islam appointed JU vice-chancellor
item.description:
Professor Md Nurul Islam of the Department of Geography and Environment has been appointed vice-chancellor of Jahangirnagar University.
The Ministry of Education issued a notification on Saturday appointing him to the post with the approval of the president and chancellor of the university.
According to the notification, Prof Nurul Islam has been relieved of his position as vice-chancellor of Dhaka Central University and appointed JU vice-chancellor under Section 11(1) of the Jahangirnagar University Act, 1973.
He will serve for four years from the date of joining or until his retirement, whichever comes earlier.
The notification, signed by Md Sultan Ahmed, assistant secretary of the General Universities Branch under the ministry's Secondary and Higher Education Division, said he would receive a salary and allowances equivalent to those of his current position and enjoy other benefits attached to the post under the rules.
As the university's chief executive officer, the new vice-chancellor will be required to reside on the university campus on a full-time basis.
Prof Nurul Islam was appointed vice-chancellor of Dhaka Central University on March 16, 2026. He also served as pro-vice-chancellor of National University from November 3, 2024.
Prof Nurul Islam obtained his PhD from the University of Nottingham in the United Kingdom in 2011. He completed his BSc (Honors) and MSc (Thesis) in Geography and Environment from Jahangirnagar University in 1992 and 1993, respectively.
