item.title: Hundreds came, bulldozers followed: Who sent them to raze Mirpur clinic?
item.description:
More than 200 people allegedly stormed a maternal and child health centre in Mirpur after midnight Thursday, tied up security guards, looted medicines and equipment and brought in heavy machinery to demolish the facility, while police now acknowledge officers were at the scene.
Four people arrested over the attack have told police they took part in exchange for money, according to Shah Ali police.
They have since been sent to jail, pushing a more consequential question to the centre of the investigation: who hired them, who organised the operation, and whether political influence helped a long-running land dispute culminate in an overnight takeover.
Local residents, businesspeople and BNP activists interviewed by Dhaka Tribune alleged that reserved-seat MP Ferdousi Ahmed Misty, a joint convener of Dhaka North BNP, led a faction seeking control of the Radda MCH-FP Centre site in Mirpur-1 and used influence over local police to facilitate the takeover.
The allegations have not been established by investigators.
Misty has denied involvement, telling media that although her name was associated with Somomona Dokandar Samabay Samiti Limited, she had no role in the vandalism and wanted police to investigate the incident according to law.
Media also reported allegations that two local BNP factions had long been seeking control of the property.
The focus on the organisers intensified after Dhaka Metropolitan Police Commissioner Mosleh Uddin Ahmed visited the devastated centre on Saturday afternoon.
After inspecting the site, the DMP chief said the extent of destruction suggested the operation could not have been carried out within half an hour or an hour.
Structures had been demolished, while equipment and machinery reported to have been inside were missing.
He said police were investigating whether there had been negligence or failure by officers during the vandalism and looting.
That question has gained significance after Shah Ali Police Station acknowledged that police were present while the demolition was underway.
The officer-in-charge confirmed the presence of police but did not provide a clear explanation as to why the attackers were not stopped or detained at the time.
According to the case filed by Radda Executive Director Dr Nasrin Akhtar, more than 200 masked people carrying locally made weapons entered the centre around midnight on Thursday after overpowering two security guards.
Medical equipment, medicines, vaccines, cash and other materials were allegedly taken before heavy machinery was used to bring down the complex.
Other reporting puts the number involved at between 200 and 250.
When Dhaka Tribune visited on Saturday, the aftermath was visible across the premises.
The Radda MCH-FP Centre after being looted and vandalized. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/Rabiul Hasan
The boundary wall had been broken, structures demolished and debris scattered across the compound.
Doors and windows had been removed or damaged, while medicines and other materials lay on the floor.
Branches of a large mango tree had also been cut.
At the main entrance, a signboard identified Somomona Dokandar Samabay Samiti Limited as the registered owner of the 10-katha plot, saying the land had been allotted by the National Housing Authority.
The cooperative insists the property belongs to it.
Md Babul, caretaker of its office at Baishakhi Bhaban in Mirpur-1, told Dhaka Tribune that the organisation had received the land from the government and had merely reclaimed possession.
The underlying ownership dispute, however, remains unresolved in the material reviewed by Dhaka Tribune.
Radda MCH-FP Centre in Mirpur-1, Dhaka, after the health centre was razed following an attack and looting. Photo: Rabiul Hasan/Dhaka Tribune
Md Saiful, who has managed the rear section of the health centre for nearly two decades, said he rushed to the area after learning that the premises were being demolished.
He estimated that around 300 people were involved, using hammers, sledgehammers and a bulldozer.
A BNP activist and businessman in the area, speaking on condition of anonymity, said he reached the site around 1am and saw several police officers before they left.
He alleged that the operation was carried out under Misty’s leadership with police assistance.
Tanvir, owner of Mirpur Surgical, alleged that people brought in from around the nearby Shah Ali shrine were used in the demolition and looting.
He said he saw no police when he reached the site.
Footpath vendor Al-Amin said the scale of the operation initially led him to believe that an official eviction drive was taking place.
“We assumed a magistrate had arrived and an eviction drive was underway,” he said.
He later saw a bulldozer demolishing the centre and alleged that some people who had gathered in the area for an urs at the Shah Ali shrine joined the vandalism and looting.
Medicines and medical supplies damaged during the looting and vandalism. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/Rabiul Hasan
Dr Nasrin Akhtar said centre officials contacted police during the attack but the facility could not be protected.
She alleged that people operating under the cooperative’s banner had been trying to take over the land for around five years and finally succeeded through Thursday night’s operation.
“We have government authorization to operate and provide healthcare services here,” she said, demanding exemplary punishment for those involved.
Radda itself says it began operations in 1974, when Radda Barnen, then Swedish Save the Children, launched a maternal and child healthcare project for disadvantaged communities in Mirpur.
Its account is supported by the organisation’s own history, while the government’s facility registry lists Radda’s Mirpur operation as an NGO clinic.
The centre provides reproductive and family planning services, antenatal and postnatal care, child immunisation, paediatric care and community health programs.
Dr Nasrin said around 400 mothers and children normally receive services there each day.
The destruction has already moved the dispute beyond competing claims over land.
On Saturday, children were being vaccinated under a tarpaulin beside the road because the facility could no longer provide normal services.
Health workers conduct measles-rubella vaccination under the open sky after the Radda MCH-FP Centre was looted and razed overnight. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/Rabiul Hasan
Dr Iqbal Jewel Majid, director of Radda’s Community Health Programme, said staff had continued administering measles vaccines despite the destruction.
“Some are waiting on chairs, while others are standing. The mothers and children are suffering in the heat,” he said.
Dr Rijuana, another physician at the centre, alleged that the land had been taken by force and said the organisation had received no government notice ordering it to leave.
She said equipment and supplies had been looted and questioned why sufficient police protection was not provided to a functioning healthcare institution.
Dr Nasrin filed a case with Shah Ali Police Station after the attack.
Police have arrested four people -- Sohel, 22, Jewel, 23, Jihad Hasan, 21, and Rabbi, 20 -- in connection with the incident.
DNCC Administrator Shafiqul Islam Khan said the government would not tolerate such incidents and instructed police to bring those responsible to justice.
The arrests establish only the alleged role of some of those who physically took part.
They do not yet answer the larger questions surrounding an operation that required hundreds of people, heavy machinery and considerable time: who mobilised and paid the attackers, who ultimately sought possession of the property, and why police present in the area failed to stop the demolition.

item.title: ‘Where will I take my children now?’
item.description:
For years, hundreds of mothers, children and low-income residents of Mirpur walked into the Radda MCH-FP Centre for vaccinations, maternal care, medical consultations and diagnostic tests. On Saturday, they returned to find their healthcare centre gone.
The buildings had been reduced to rubble, equipment and medical supplies were allegedly looted, and the only healthcare still available was being delivered under a tarpaulin beside the road.
A midnight attack on the Radda MCH-FP Centre in Mirpur-1 has left an immediate human toll beyond the destruction of the facility itself: around 300-400 patients who relied on it every day must now look elsewhere for care, according to centre officials.
Radda MCH-FP Centre in Mirpur-1, Dhaka, after the health centre was razed following an attack and looting. Photo: Rabiul Hasan/Dhaka Tribune
The centre’s regular services remained suspended on Saturday. Patients arriving for consultations, ultrasounds, maternal and child healthcare, family planning and other services were being turned away.
Only the government’s measles-rubella vaccination campaign continued, with health workers setting up tables and chairs outside the demolished facility.
By 2pm, 21 children had been vaccinated there.
“Those who do not know about the situation are coming here for services,” Radda Executive Director Nasrin Akhter told Dhaka Tribune.
“Some are coming for vaccination, while others are coming for ultrasound and other healthcare services. But as everything has been broken and looted, we are asking them to go to other centres.”
The centre had four doctors and around 15 nurses, paramedics and other health workers, she said. They are now able to provide only vaccinations.
For regular patients, the rubble represents something less abstract than a land dispute: the sudden disappearance of a familiar and affordable source of healthcare.
Momtaz Begum, a Mirpur resident who regularly brought her children to Radda, stood shocked before the destroyed facility.
“I used to bring my children here regularly. I knew many of the health workers. Where will I take my children now? There is no good healthcare centre nearby,” she told Dhaka Tribune.
“I came here today and was shocked. How could the entire hospital be broken down within a few hours? Nobody said anything. What kind of country are we living in?”
Another mother arrived to have her child vaccinated without knowing what had happened.
“If I had known, I would not have come here,” she said. “Earlier, I brought my child here and received vaccines inside the centre.”
On Saturday, mothers and children instead waited in the heat beneath a temporary tarpaulin.
The scene underscored the consequences of Thursday night’s attack: above the makeshift vaccination tables hung a banner asserting Somomona Dokandar Samabaya Samiti Limited’s ownership of the property.
Three such banners were visible around the premises.
Centre Director Iqbal Jillul Majid said Radda had long been a major healthcare provider for disadvantaged residents of Mirpur.
“It was a major support for the poorest people in this area,” he said. “Not only the poor, but also people from better-off families came here for different needs. I never imagined that someone would break it down like this.”
The centre says all 15 rooms at the facility were destroyed.
A doctor’s chamber after the Radda center was looted and razed, with even the windows removed. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/Rabiul Hasan
“Not a single room remains. They broke everything down and took everything away,” Majid said.
Radda’s Mirpur operation is listed in the government’s facility registry as an NGO clinic.
Available institutional records and contemporary reports indicate that its maternal and child healthcare activities in Mirpur began in 1974.
Health worker Farzana said the destruction had also disrupted basic record-keeping.
“We have no documents left here. It has also become difficult to keep track of how many children we are vaccinating,” she said.
According to Radda officials, the missing items include government EPI vaccines and registers, family-planning supplies, medicines, two ultrasound machines, computers, printers, refrigerators, a generator, air conditioners, CCTV cameras, furniture and other equipment.
Medicines and medical supplies damaged during the looting and vandalism. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/Rabiul Hasan
Showly Rahman, a Mirpur-10 resident, said she had visited Radda more than 20 times, particularly for her children’s vaccinations.
“Radda is a very reliable and beneficial institution for low-income, middle-income and working people,” she said.
Vaccines, she said, were reliably available at the centre at affordable prices when the same vaccines could cost considerably more elsewhere.
Roadside shopkeeper Yasin Arafat said he had watched hundreds of patients arrive at the centre during the seven years he had worked nearby.
“So many poor people used to come here and receive healthcare. Then suddenly it was broken down,” he said.
The disruption followed an attack around midnight on Thursday in which more than 200 masked people allegedly entered the centre carrying locally made weapons, restrained security guards and looted medical equipment and other belongings before heavy machinery was used to demolish the structures.
The broad outline of the attack is consistent with other reporting, although ownership of the land remains disputed.
A case has been filed with Shah Ali Police Station, and four people have been arrested.
Police said the arrested suspects admitted participating in the attack in exchange for money.
Shah Ali police also acknowledged that officers were present while the vandalism was taking place, although questions remain over why they did not stop it.
DMP Commissioner Mosleh Uddin Ahmed has formed a three-member committee to determine whether police negligence contributed to the destruction.
After inspecting the site, he said the scale of damage suggested the operation continued for a considerable period rather than just 30 minutes or an hour.
Police are also investigating allegations concerning reserved-seat MP Ferdousi Ahmed Misty.
She has denied involvement in the vandalism.
Somomona Dokandar Samabaya Samiti Limited claims ownership of the property, but Dhaka Tribune could not obtain its detailed response.
Its listed office at Boishakhi Super Market could not be located despite inquiries, while a shop associated with the cooperative was open but unattended.
A signboard of Somomona Dokandar Samabay Samiti Limited hangs at the entrance of the Radda MCH-FP Centre after it was looted and razed, while health workers administer measles-rubella vaccines below it. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/Rabiul Hasan
Radda officials maintain that if another party had a legitimate claim over the property, the dispute should have been resolved through legal and administrative channels rather than by destroying a functioning health facility.
“If they had a claim over this land, they could have contacted us,” Akhter said. “Instead, they came at night and broke down the entire institution.”
Whatever ultimately emerges from the ownership dispute and criminal investigation, the immediate consequence was already visible on Saturday: children receiving vaccines beneath a tarpaulin, patients being sent elsewhere and a healthcare centre that had served Mirpur’s residents for around five decades lying in ruins.

item.title: ‘I had a father. Now I have neither’
item.description:
“I have become an orphan. Who will I stay with now? Everyone else has parents. I didn’t have a mother before, but I had a father. Now I have neither.”
Nine-year-old Arfa struggled through tears as she tried to make sense of a loss far bigger than the numbers Bangladesh records every day in its worsening dengue outbreak.
Her father, Tajul Islam Taju, died on September 18 after contracting dengue. He was the only parent Arfa had ever known.
Her mother died just five days after giving birth to her.
For Arfa, therefore, her father’s death was not simply another addition to the country’s dengue toll.
It took away the person who had been both mother and father to her -- the man who took her to school, brought her home, took her out on holidays and built his life around raising his only daughter.
“When friends were picked up by their mothers at school, I used to feel sad and miss having a mother,” Arfa told Dhaka Tribune.
“But my father used to come to pick me up. Even without a mother, I felt comforted knowing I had my father. Now, even he is gone. Father will never take me to school or out for an outing again.”
Her loss comes as dengue is exacting an increasingly heavy toll across Bangladesh.
At least 214 people have died and 70,104 have been hospitalised with dengue this year through September 25, according to the Directorate General of Health Services.
Another 955 patients were admitted to hospitals and three died in the latest 24-hour reporting period.
September alone has accounted for 115 deaths in its first 25 days, making it the deadliest month of 2026 so far.
Behind one of those deaths is a child in Rampura now asking where she belongs.
Arfa was born by Caesarean section at Narail Sadar Hospital on February 13, 2018.
Five days later, her mother Marufa suddenly collapsed while still recovering after childbirth. According to the family, she suffered severe bleeding and died.
Arfa grew up without any memory of her mother.
Tajul never remarried. Instead, according to his family, he devoted himself to raising his daughter at their home in the Wapda Road area of Rampura, where they lived with her grandparents.
Every school day, he would take Arfa to school and bring her home. On holidays, he took her out.
His mother, Sakhina Begum, said Tajul’s illness began after he returned home from his shop late at night with a fever and feeling unwell.
The following morning, despite still being sick, one of his first concerns was his daughter.
“Mom, will you take Arfa to school, or should I?” Sakhina recalled him asking after Fajr prayers.
She told him to rest and took Arfa herself.
By around 7am, Tajul’s condition had worsened. He began vomiting repeatedly after eating a banana and some bread.
The family initially tried to persuade him to go to hospital, but he believed he would recover. He later consulted a doctor and returned home with prescribed medication and intravenous saline.
Nine-year-old Arfa loses her only parent to dengue as Bangladesh’s 2026 death toll reaches 214. Photo: Abir Ahmmed Shupto/Dhaka Tribune
By evening, however, the vomiting had intensified and he developed chest pain.
He was rushed to Khidmah Hospital, but doctors there recommended transferring him to a facility with intensive-care capacity.
Tajul was subsequently admitted to Better Life Hospital, where tests confirmed dengue at around 8pm, according to his family.
By then, his condition was critical. His blood pressure had fallen, he was having difficulty breathing and the vomiting continued.
When his mother saw him the following morning, she realised how seriously ill he had become.
“I could tell just by looking at him that my son’s time was running out,” Sakhina said, breaking down in tears.
As his condition deteriorated further, Tajul was transferred to Evercare Hospital and placed on life support.
He died at 7:55pm on September 18.
He was buried the following day in the family graveyard at his ancestral home in Debidwar, Cumilla.
Throughout her father’s illness, Arfa had waited for him to return.
Farhana Akter, an aunt of Arfa’s late mother, said the family tried to reassure the child.
“Arfa had been crying ever since Taju bhai fell ill. We kept telling her that her father would get better,” she said.
When the news finally came that he had died, there was no longer anything they could tell her.
“The child became inconsolable,” Farhana said. “There wasn’t a single person who could hold back tears upon seeing her.”
Arfa’s grandfather has now taken responsibility for raising her.
“My granddaughter wasn’t an orphan until now; losing her father has made her one,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
“I will look after her now. I am getting on in years, though, so I don’t know how much I’ll be able to do.”
For Arfa, the statistics of Bangladesh’s dengue outbreak have been reduced to something much simpler.
She once watched other children leave school with their mothers and wished she had one too. But her father would arrive, and that was enough.
Now, as Bangladesh counts 214 dengue deaths, Arfa is learning what one of those deaths means when the person behind the number was the only parent she had left.

item.title: 1,415 rivers, but how many are truly alive?
item.description:
Bangladesh has officially counted 1,415 rivers, but knowing how many waterways the country has done little to arrest a deepening crisis threatening their flow, ecology and the livelihoods of millions of people.
From the Buriganga and Shitalakkhya around Dhaka to the Karnaphuli in Chittagong and Kopotakkho in the southwest, rivers are struggling under mounting pressure from encroachment, industrial pollution, siltation, unplanned development, declining dry-season flows and the effects of climate change.
The consequences extend far beyond the rivers themselves.
Agriculture, fisheries, navigation, biodiversity, public health and the livelihoods of river-dependent communities are all increasingly at risk.
The government published a comprehensive national inventory in April 2025 identifying 1,415 rivers.
The list was prepared through a process involving the Ministry of Water Resources, Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB), National River Conservation Commission (NRCC), local administrations and river activists.
The government reiterated the figure in Parliament in June this year.
But experts say counting the rivers is only the beginning.
A meaningful national river database, they argue, must establish boundaries and regularly track water flows, pollution, navigability, ecological conditions and encroachment.
Without that information, assessing degradation and designing effective restoration programs will remain difficult.
The Buriganga, Turag, Balu and Shitalakkhya surrounding the capital have for years faced industrial pollution, untreated sewage, solid waste, encroachment and rapid urbanisation.
The Buriganga, once central to Dhaka’s trade and transport, has become one of the most visible examples of the country’s river crisis. Industrial effluent, untreated sewage, plastic and other waste have severely affected water quality in sections of the river.
The Turag and Balu face similar pressure from urbanisation, waste dumping and occupation of riverbanks, while industrial activity along the Shitalakkhya has heightened concerns over wastewater entering the river.
The problem is not confined to Dhaka.
The Karnaphuli, crucial to Chittagong and the country’s principal seaport, faces pressures from industrialisation, urban expansion, port activities and waste.
The Halda, one of the country’s ecologically important natural breeding grounds for freshwater fish, is vulnerable to pollution, altered flows and disruption of its aquatic environment.
Siltation presents another major challenge.
Sediment accumulation can reduce river depth, restrict flows and navigation and aggravate drainage congestion and waterlogging.
The Kopotakkho in southwestern Bangladesh is among the rivers associated with persistent navigability and waterlogging problems.
Dredging is frequently prescribed as the solution, but water experts warn that excavation alone cannot restore rivers sustainably.
They say dredging must be based on scientific assessments of sediment movement, river morphology, upstream conditions and connections among rivers, canals, wetlands and floodplains.
Without addressing disrupted flows and the underlying causes of sedimentation, repeated dredging may provide only temporary relief.
Bangladesh’s river crisis also extends beyond its borders.
The country officially has 57 transboundary rivers, 54 shared with India and three with Myanmar.
As a downstream country, Bangladesh is particularly vulnerable to upstream water management.
Withdrawals, dams and other interventions can alter the volume and timing of water reaching its rivers, affecting irrigation, fisheries, navigation and ecosystems.
The 1996 Ganges Water Sharing Treaty provides a framework for dry-season sharing of the Ganges, while management of the Teesta and other shared waterways remains a major transboundary challenge.
Experts say stronger water diplomacy, transparent data sharing and basin-wide cooperation are essential, alongside maintaining the environmental flows rivers require to survive.
Climate change is adding another layer of pressure.
Changing rainfall, flash floods, upstream runoff, sea-level rise and salinity intrusion are altering river systems.
In coastal areas, salinity threatens freshwater ecosystems, agriculture and drinking-water sources, while sudden upstream surges can devastate communities and farmland in northern and northeastern Bangladesh.
Experts caution, however, against blaming climate change for a crisis also driven by human actions. Encroachment, pollution, unplanned infrastructure and poor water management can magnify climate impacts.
Water and environmental expert Professor Ainun Nishat said Bangladesh needs an integrated, basin-wide approach that protects natural flows and addresses interconnected water systems rather than treating individual rivers as isolated entities.
Professor Dr Md Sabbir Mostafa Khan, chairman of Dhaka WASA and professor and head of BUET’s Department of Water Resources Engineering, echoed that assessment.
“River management must consider entire river basins and interconnected water flows rather than focusing on individual waterways,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
“Without ensuring natural river flows, controlling encroachment and pollution, and integrating water management with urban planning, river conservation initiatives will not be effective in the long term.”
He called for a reliable national database reconciling inventories maintained by different government agencies, digital mapping of river boundaries, tougher action against encroachment and pollution and protection of canals, wetlands and floodplains.
Scientific assessments of water and sediment flows should precede dredging projects, he said, while stronger water diplomacy is needed to protect transboundary rivers.
Bangladesh already has a powerful legal foundation for river protection.
In a landmark 2019 judgment involving the Turag, the High Court accorded rivers the status of legal or living entities and designated the NRCC their legal guardian. The full judgment extended that status to all rivers in the country.
Yet effective protection remains a challenge.
Bangladesh River Foundation Chairman Mohammad Monir Hossain said implementation of the court’s recognition had yet to be fully ensured.
“Recognising rivers as living entities is an important step, but protecting them requires more than government initiatives. Effective and coordinated participation from all relevant stakeholders is essential,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
He called for cooperation among ministries, local administrations, elected representatives, civil society, NGOs, industries, educational and religious institutions and river-dependent communities.
Buriganga Riverkeeper and Waterkeepers Bangladesh Coordinator Sharif Jamil said the stakes extend beyond protecting individual waterways.
“Rivers are the lifelines of our forests, ecosystems and communities,” he said. “Protecting rivers means protecting water, livelihoods and life itself.”
For a country shaped by rivers, experts say the challenge is therefore no longer simply identifying how many remain on the map, but ensuring that those 1,415 rivers remain flowing, functioning ecosystems rather than names on a government list.

item.title: Mohammadpur office vandalized, looted amid alleged property seizure attempt
item.description:
An office in Mohammadpur’s Chand Uddan Housing area was allegedly vandalized and looted on Saturday morning amid an alleged attempt to seize the property.
Zainal Abedin filed a written complaint with police, saying the incident took place at around 10am at the Mohammadpur Twin Tower office in the Beribadh area.
In the complaint, Zainal said 100 to 150 unidentified people illegally entered the office on the 2nd floor by breaking the door, lock and windows. They allegedly searched different rooms and the storeroom before loading Tk15 lakh in cash, 5 laptops, 2 air conditioners, 3 CCTV cameras, office furniture and other equipment onto a truck and taking them away.
He further alleged that Md Mostaqur Rahman Khokon Chowdhury, 62, along with Mahin, Prince and Alamin, had been conspiring for some time to seize the office with the help of local individuals.
According to the complaint, the incident disrupted the office’s normal operations and resulted in financial and administrative losses, while important official documents and information were also at risk of being lost.
Additional Deputy Commissioner of Police (ADC) for Tejgaon Zone Md Jewel Rana said an unwanted incident occurred on land adjacent to Rose Villa in Chand Uddan, west of Beribadh.
He said Alam had been in possession of the land for a long time. During the incident, around 150 to 200 people, led by Jony and Rezaul, allegedly entered the land, broke down the tin fencing, vandalized the office and attempted to seize the land by installing new tin fencing around its boundary.
Jewel Rana also said both parties claimed to have documents supporting their ownership of the land.

item.title: Sarah Karim couture opens new showroom at Centerpoint Mall
item.description:
Fashion designer Sarah Karim’s couture house has opened a new showroom at Centerpoint Mall in Uttara, bringing its signature craftsmanship and contemporary designs closer to customers in northern Dhaka.
The showroom was formally inaugurated at 5pm on Saturday.
The new outlet features Sarah Karim couture’s collections of bridal, occasion and formal wear, with its signature emphasis on intricate craftsmanship and contemporary interpretations of traditional designs.
Sarah Karim Couture’s new showroom at Centerpoint Mall in Uttara, Dhaka, officially opened on Saturday, September 26, 2026. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Speaking to the Dhaka Tribune during the launch, designer Sarah Karim said the decision to open the showroom in Uttara was driven partly by a desire to make couture more accessible to customers living in the northern part of the city, where navigating Dhaka’s traffic can often be challenging.
“We currently work with over 250 traditional artisans specialising in zardozi, ari and gota patti,” Karim said.
“Expanding our retail presence directly sustains their craftsmanship while making high-end fashion accessible to both our long-standing patrons and a younger demographic in northern Dhaka,” she added.
Sarah Karim Couture’s new showroom at Centerpoint Mall in Uttara, Dhaka, officially opened on Saturday, September 26, 2026. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
The new showroom has been designed to reflect the brand’s distinctive aesthetic, creating a dedicated space where customers can explore its latest collections and select outfits in a refined setting.
Sarah Karim is a recognised name in Bangladesh’s couture fashion scene, particularly for combining traditional craftsmanship with contemporary silhouettes and designs.
Her journey in fashion was shaped by a family initiative that worked to support traditional artisans and provide them with employment opportunities. Through close collaboration with artisans, she became familiar with techniques such as zardozi, ari and gota patti.
These traditional techniques later became an important part of her design language. Karim incorporated handwork and traditional motifs into contemporary cuts, silhouettes and colour palettes, creating a distinct aesthetic for Sarah Karim couture.
The brand’s collections include bridal and occasion wear with detailed hand embroidery and intricate craftsmanship forming a key part of its designs.
The new Uttara showroom carries forward that approach, bringing the brand’s collections to a wider customer base while maintaining its focus on traditional craftsmanship.
Sarah Karim Couture’s new showroom at Centerpoint Mall in Uttara, Dhaka, officially opened on Saturday, September 26, 2026. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
For Karim, fashion is closely connected to preserving traditional craftsmanship and creating sustainable opportunities for artisans.
The designer currently works with more than 250 traditional artisans specializing in different forms of handcraft, including zardozi, ari and gota patti.
Through its growing retail presence, Sarah Karim couture aims to create greater opportunities to showcase and sustain these traditional skills while introducing them to contemporary customers.
The designer has also been involved in initiatives related to women’s empowerment, artisan livelihoods and support for disadvantaged children.
Sarah Karim couture has participated in fashion events in Bangladesh and abroad, while its customer base has gradually expanded beyond the country.
Sarah Karim Couture’s new showroom at Centerpoint Mall in Uttara, Dhaka, officially opened on Saturday, September 26, 2026. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
The brand’s design philosophy centres on preserving valuable craft traditions passed down through generations while adapting them to contemporary tastes.
With the new showroom at Centerpoint Mall, Sarah Karim couture is looking to further connect this heritage with modern fashion and make its collections more accessible to customers in Uttara and surrounding areas.

item.title: PM arrives in Dubai en route to Dhaka after attending UNGA session
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman arrived Dubai on Saturday on his way back home after wrapping up a five-day visit to New York to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, where he highlighted Bangladesh's positions on global peace, climate change, the Rohingya crisis and other issues of international concern.
"An Emirates flight carrying the prime minister, his wife Dr Zubaida Rahman and members of his entourage arrived at Dubai International Airport at 8:23pm (Dubai time)," PM's Deputy Press Secretary Hasan Shiplu told BSS.
He is scheduled to leave Dubai for Dhaka by Emirates flight EK582 at 2am on Sunday and will arrive at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport at 8:40am the same day.
The prime minister left New York on Friday (New York time) after delivering his maiden address to the General Debate of the 81st UNGA and completing a packed program of bilateral and high-level engagements with world leaders, UN officials, development partners and representatives of international organizations.
During his four-day program in New York, Tarique Rahman held 30 official engagements, including bilateral meetings with 11 countries, Prime Minister's Adviser and PMO spokesperson Mahdi Amin said at a press briefing before the prime minister's departure.
The engagements focused on Bangladesh's national interests, trade and investment, manpower exports, energy security, regional cooperation, the Rohingya crisis, health, climate change and international peace.
The prime minister took part in eight UNGA-related engagements, four high-level events on the sidelines of the UNGA and 11 bilateral meetings, besides meetings with international organizations and prominent personalities, Mahdi said.
In his UNGA address, Tarique Rahman reaffirmed Bangladesh's support for global humanity and world peace and called for conflicts to be resolved through dialogue, diplomacy and mutual cooperation.
He also pledged to build a prosperous, self-reliant and welfare-oriented democratic Bangladesh by ensuring political and economic empowerment and equal opportunities for all, while outlining the government's 3-R strategy of Recovery, Restoration and Reconstruction.
The prime minister put the Rohingya crisis prominently before the international community, calling for safe, voluntary and dignified repatriation and stronger international cooperation.
During the visit, he discussed the issue with UN Secretary-General's Special Envoy on Myanmar Julie Bishop and UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih.
Bishop and the prime minister discussed the need for international cooperation for a dignified return and a sustainable solution, while Salih stressed continued international cooperation and appreciated Bangladesh's humanitarian role.
Tarique Rahman also met UN Secretary-General Ant¢nio Guterres, who, according to Mahdi Amin, expressed gratitude for Bangladesh's role in sheltering the Rohingyas and contributing troops to UN peacekeeping operations and appreciated the country's role in climate resilience and multilateral affairs.
The prime minister's bilateral engagements included meetings with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Bhutanese Prime Minister Dasho Tshering Tobgay, Maldives Vice-President Uz Hussain Mohamed Latheef, Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aim‚, Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic and Pakistani Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif.
With Erdogan, he discussed expanding Bangladesh-Turkiye trade and investment and diversifying economic cooperation. With the leaders of Bhutan and the Maldives, he discussed strengthening bilateral relations and expanding cooperation, while his meeting with Haiti's prime minister covered bilateral relations and regional and international cooperation.
In his meeting with World Bank Group President Ajay Banga, the prime minister discussed Bangladesh's development priorities and economic progress, including strengthening cooperation with the World Bank and exploring new areas of partnership.
On climate change, the prime minister called for collective global action at the "Climate Action and the Just Transition" meeting and later called for four urgent actions to tackle sea-level rise: faster emission cuts, accessible adaptation finance, wider access to climate-smart technologies and stronger international cooperation.
At a high-level event on maternal, newborn health and midwifery, he outlined his government's plan to build a "Healthy Bangladesh" centred on primary healthcare, including the recruitment of 100,000 additional health workers and 25,000 professional midwives.
The prime minister's economic engagements also included a meeting with Gates Foundation CEO Mark Suzman on public health and healthcare modernization and discussions with international philanthropic and humanitarian organizations on humanitarian challenges, climate change, sustainable development and economic partnership.
Before leaving New York, Tarique Rahman attended a breakfast meeting with top Wall Street investors hosted by JPMorgan Chase, where investment opportunities in different sectors of Bangladesh and ways to increase investment were discussed.
He also held a meeting with the president of the International Peace Institute, where Bangladesh's return to democratic rule was welcomed and its role in promoting global peace was discussed.
On Friday, the prime minister also held bilateral meetings with the Crown Prince of Kuwait, the Saudi foreign minister and the deputy prime minister and foreign minister of the United Arab Emirates.
The three countries invited Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to visit their respective countries, while the meetings discussed protecting the interests of Bangladeshi workers, increasing manpower exports, energy security, cooperation in the mineral sector and increasing investment in Bangladesh.
Biman Bangladesh Airlines also signed an agreement to purchase 11 Boeing aircraft during the visit as Bangladesh moves to expand its aviation sector and open new international routes.
Prime Minister's wife Dr Zubaida Rahman also took part in eight high-level engagements during the visit, delivering remarks at four of them, including the UN General Assembly's Platform of Women Leaders, the First Spouses' Dialogue and a high-level event on maternal and child health and midwifery.

item.title: CUET students continue protests demanding VC’s reinstatement
item.description:
Students of Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) continued protests on Saturday, demanding the reinstatement of former Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr Abu Sadat Mohammad Sayem.
They drew protest graffiti across the campus, staged a procession and showed a “red card” to newly appointed VC Prof Sheikh Shariful Alam.
Since on Saturday morning, students painted protest slogans and satirical graffiti on academic buildings and other prominent spots. “We will continue the movement until a gazette is issued reinstating Prof Sayem as vice-chancellor. We will not return to classes until our demand is met,” said CUET student Ridwanul Haque.
On September 21, the government removed Prof Sayem and appointed Prof Sheikh Shariful Alam of Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (KUET) as his replacement.
Prof Sayem had been appointed CUET VC on July 27, just 56 days before his removal. Students began protesting that night. They have been observing a “complete shutdown” at the university since September 22 as part of the ongoing protests.
